blocks.text: Using microwave equipment with a wavelength of 2.8 cm (Fig 15.6), an interference pattern can be observed. The microwave transmitter is directed at a double gap in a metal barrier. The microwaves are diffracted at the two gaps and spread out into the region beyond, where they are detected with a probe receiver. Moving the probe around finds regions of high intensity (constructive interference) and low intensity (destructive interference). The probe may be connected to a meter, or to an audio amplifier and loudspeaker to give an audible output.

blocks.alt: A bench seen from above. On the left a microwave transmitter points at a row of metal sheets that leave two narrow gaps. Beyond the gaps on the right is a microwave probe, wired to a meter.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.6: Microwaves can also be used to show interference effects (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.6).

blocks.text: A simple way to show interference of light is to shine a laser through two slits (Fig 15.7): two clear lines on a black slide, separated by a fraction of a millimetre. On the screen a series of equally spaced dots of light, called interference fringes, appears where waves from the two slits arrive in phase (constructive interference); the dark regions between are the result of destructive interference. These bright and dark fringes correspond to the loud and quiet regions of the two loudspeakers.

blocks.alt: A laser box with a yellow warning label sends a red beam to a glass slide with a double slit. From the slits eight red lines spread to a screen, where they end in a row of equally spaced red dots.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.7: Light beams from the two slits interfere in the space beyond (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.7).

blocks.text: We can check that light reaches the screen from both slits. Mark a point at a dark fringe, then cover one slit so that light passes through only one. The fringes disappear and a broad band of light, the diffraction pattern of a single slit, appears; the point that was dark is now bright. Covering the other slit instead gives the same effect. So light arrives from both slits, but at the dark fringes the two beams cancel. A bright bulb can give similar results, but a laser is more convenient because its light is concentrated into a narrow, intense beam. Thomas Young had no laser when he first did the experiment in 1801.
